messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Emily is a 43-year-old European American chef in a stable relationship. Several years ago, she was diagnosed with a life-threatening illness that required immediate and aggressive treatment. The experience left her feeling overwhelmed by grief and an overwhelming sense of vulnerability. Since then, Emily has come to believe that her body will never fully recover from the trauma of her illness, and that it is now permanently damaged and vulnerable. This belief has led her to engage in various maladaptive strategies to cope with her distress. She often avoids situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, fearing they would only remind her of what she can no longer experience normally. Emily also frequently stays up late into the night, unable to relax even when she knows she is safe. Emily's sense of vulnerability has intensified her threat perceptions; she feels as though her body reacts to perceived danger before she has a chance to process it rationally. This heightened state of alertness makes it difficult for her to feel truly relaxed, even in familiar and secure environments. The constant fear that her illness could return or that her body might fail her at any moment fuels her avoidance behaviors. Her memories of the traumatic event are vivid and distressing. When these memories resurface, they come with full sensory intensity—Emily feels like she is reliving every moment of her ordeal. This intense recollection often leaves her feeling overwhelmed by grief. The extremity of these memories makes it hard for Emily to believe that such an experience actually happened to her. The relentless cycle has taken its toll on Emily's emotional state and daily life as a chef. She finds herself increasingly withdrawn, numbing her feelings to avoid the pain of remembering or anticipating another crisis. Her late nights have affected her energy levels and focus at work, leading to several minor mistakes that she attributes to her ongoing distress. Emily’s belief that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again has further exacerbated her avoidance behaviors and increased her sense of threat. This feedback loop has made it difficult for her to function normally in her daily life and maintain her usual level of performance at work. Recently, a particularly vivid flashback during a routine shift at the restaurant pushed Emily over the edge. She felt as if she were right back in that harrowing moment, unable to breathe or think clearly. This episode, combined with her growing sense of isolation and inability to cope effectively, finally prompted her to seek help. Emily is most afraid of never being able to reclaim a normal life, free from constant fear and grief. She hopes for relief from the overwhelming sense of vulnerability and a return to feeling emotionally connected to the world around her.
